sections.skill: Recalculate or estimate numbers before relying on them

questions.prompt: In this fictional example, what is the correct total?
questions.intro: Language models can make arithmetic and counting mistakes, sometimes inside an otherwise good answer. A total may not match its parts, a percentage may be calculated from the wrong base, units may be mixed (minutes and hours), or a rounded number may be treated as exact. When a number matters, CHECK IT: redo simple arithmetic yourself or with a calculator, ESTIMATE whether the size makes sense ("a month of groceries for 1,000 dollars is plausible; 100,000 is not"), and confirm that units match. Some products can run a calculation tool, but you should still check results that matter.

example.label: Fictional example (prepared in advance; not a real AI output)

example.response: Notebooks: 3 x 4.50 = 13.50 dollars. Pens: 2 x 1.25 = 2.50 dollars. Total: 13.50 + 2.50 = 17.00 dollars.

questions.prompt: What is 4 x 7.50?
questions.intro: Two quick skills check most numbers. RECALCULATE: redo the arithmetic yourself, one step at a time. Example: 4 tickets at 7.50 dollars: 4 x 7.50 = 30.00 dollars. ESTIMATE: round the numbers and see if the answer is in the right range. Example: 19 x 21 is about 20 x 20 = 400, so an answer of 3,990 is clearly wrong. Also check UNITS: 30 minutes is 0.5 hours, not 30 hours. A wrong unit can make a number look reasonable when it is not.

sections.skill: Find errors in multi-step and percentage answers

questions.prompt: A tool computed a project cost in four tidy steps, but used 12 workers instead of your 21. What should you check first?

choices.text: Whether the final number is rounded
Whether the steps are neatly formatted
Whether the answer is long enough
Whether it used your actual input figures

questions.correct_answer: Whether it used your actual input figures
questions.intro: Number errors often hide in multi-step answers: one wrong step early on makes every later number wrong while the reasoning still looks tidy. Check the inputs first (did it use your actual figures?), then each step, then the final number. Watch percentage traps: a 50 percent rise followed by a 50 percent fall does not return to the start. And be careful with very precise-looking results from uncertain inputs: "12.37 percent" built on a guessed number is still a guess.
questions.feedback: Wrong inputs make every later step wrong.
